answer: The statute provides that “The registration of title to every land parcel under this Act shall be in accordance with the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.” So, for a parcel being brought under the title-registration system, the registration of title must follow the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.

The Commissioner of Title Settlement must, on receipt of the certified copies of cadastral maps, “publish a Notice in the Gazette,” and that Notice must call for any claimants to the land parcel specified in the Notice to submit their claims to him “within a prescribed period from the date of publication of such Notice.” After claims are made in response to that Notice, the Commissioner of Title Settlement must “cause an investigation to be conducted” to determine the “genuinness or otherwise of claims.”

Applied here, because the Commissioner has received certified copies of cadastral maps, he must publish the Gazette Notice inviting claims within the prescribed period, and once claims are received, he must have an investigation conducted to determine whether those claims are genuine or not.

The provisions create two different procedures.

1. **Reference of disputed claims for determination**: Under section 21, if during the investigations the Commissioner of Title Settlement forms the opinion that, because the claims are disputed, it would be more appropriate for the investigations to be carried out by the District Court, the Commissioner of Title Settlement **may refer such claims for investigation and determination to the District Court** having jurisdiction over the area where the land is situate.

2. **Appeal by an aggrieved claimant**: Under section 22, **any claimant aggrieved by any Declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14** may **prefer an appeal** against that declaration **within the prescribed period** to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land parcel is situate.

So, the first procedure is a **Commissioner-initiated reference** of disputed claims during the investigation stage, while the second is a **claimant-initiated appeal** against a declaration, and it must be brought within the prescribed period.

Rule: For land parcels registered under the Registration of Title Act, a person acquiring an interest is not entitled to that title or interest unless it is registered. Also, land or any interest in it may be transferred or dealt with only in accordance with the Act, and any disposition otherwise effected is void. An instrument pertaining to land executed in accordance with the Act takes effect only on registration.

Application: Nimal’s instrument was not registered under the Act. Therefore, the transferee did not acquire the interest, because the Act says there is no entitlement to the title or interest unless it is registered. The parties’ private agreement alone did not make the transfer effective, because the instrument takes effect only on registration, and a disposition otherwise effected is void.

The governing rule is that, "Except in accordance with the provisions of this Act, an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under this Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act."

Applied here, the registered owner executes one instrument purporting to convey the parcel to two purchasers as owners in common. That is an instrument made in favour of two or more persons in common. On the facts given, and absent anything showing it is made in accordance with the Act, the instrument is void and it shall not be registered under the Registration of Title Act.

The statutory rule is that, for land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, “The Prescription Ordinance (Chapter 68) shall not apply” and “The Partition Act shall not apply.”

Applied here, the parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership. Therefore, a claim of ownership through prescription cannot be based on the Prescription Ordinance for that parcel, and the Partition Act does not apply to that parcel, so a partition action under that Act cannot be maintained in relation to it.

The rule is that, subject to section 60, a Court may order rectification where a registration has been obtained by fraud, but the Court “shall not order the rectification of a register so as to affect the title of a registered owner who is in possession and who has acquired the land parcel or interest therein for valuable consideration, unless such owner was a party to such fraud.”

Applied here, the registration was obtained by fraud, but the present registered owner is in possession, acquired the parcel for valuable consideration, and was not a party to the fraud. So the Court may not order rectification against that owner’s title.

As to indemnity, a person suffering loss or damage or who has been prejudiced by reason of “not rectifying the Register in consequence of an order of Court made under section 59” is, on an order of Court, entitled to be indemnified by the Government out of the Insurance Fund. There is no stated fact that the person who suffered loss caused or substantially contributed to the fraud or derives title from such a person, so section 60(2) does not on these facts bar indemnity. Accordingly, the person who suffered loss may claim indemnity, provided the loss was by reason of non-rectification in consequence of a court order under section 59.

The statutory rule is that, once the Superintendent of Surveys is satisfied that the condominium plan conforms to the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and the Registration of Title Act, he must certify the plan on behalf of the Surveyor-General and then (a) file the original of the condominium plan after making a suitable reference on the cadastral map used for registration of title, and (b) forward the duplicate of the condominium plan and the owner’s application to the appropriate Registrar of Title. If the Registrar of Title is satisfied that the application conforms to the same laws, he must (a) file the duplicate of the condominium plan in the Parcels File, (b) open a new title register for each condominium parcel shown on the plan and make suitable cross-references in the register in which the land parcel is registered, (c) record in the Property Section that the land comprised therein consists only of common property, (d) record in the Encumbrances Section that registers in respect of condominium parcels have been opened, (e) inform the applicant that the condominium parcels have been registered and notify him of the reference numbers of the relevant registers, and (f) issue a Certificate of Title after recovery of the prescribed fees.

Applied here, because the condominium plan has been approved as conforming to the applicable laws, the Superintendent should certify it, file the original with the required cadastral-map reference, and send the duplicate and application to the Registrar. The Registrar should then file the duplicate in the Parcels File, open a separate title register for each condominium parcel with cross-references, make the required entries in the Property Section and Encumbrances Section, notify the applicant of registration and the reference numbers, and issue the Certificate of Title after collecting the prescribed fees.

The governing rule is:
- “When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.”
- “Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.”
- “Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.”

Applying those rules here:
1. The surviving spouse takes one-half of the intestate estate.
2. The remaining one-half goes to descendants, because descendants are the first class after the spouse’s right.
3. There is one living child and one deceased child represented by two grandchildren. The living child takes a share equally with the deceased child’s branch, and the two grandchildren take that deceased child’s branch per stirpes/by representation.

Calculation of the remaining half:
- Estate remaining after spouse’s share = 1/2
- There are 2 branches among descendants: the living child’s branch and the deceased child’s branch
- Each branch gets 1/2 of the remaining half = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 of the whole estate

So the shares are:
- Surviving spouse: 1/2
- Living child: 1/4
- Each grandchild: the deceased child’s 1/4 branch is divided between the 2 grandchildren, so 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8 each

Order of succession: spouse first to one-half; then descendants, with children taking equally per capita and the issue of a deceased child taking per stirpes/by representation.

The rule in s 5 is that a will made beyond Sri Lanka that contains a devise or disposition of immovable property situate within Sri Lanka will be “valid and effectual to alienate and pass” that immovable property if it was “duly made and executed according to and in conformity with the forms and solemnities prescribed by the law of the country where the same shall have been so made and executed” and was made by a person who is “competent to make a will” by the law of that country or of Sri Lanka. On the facts, the will was executed outside Sri Lanka, it complies with the formalities of the country of execution, and the testator was competent under that country’s law. Therefore, the foreign will is capable of validly passing the Sri Lankan immovable property.

Before any precept or order for the service of notice or summons is issued in proceedings to enforce a right of pre-emption, proof must be furnished to the court that the proceedings or action have been registered as a lis pendens in accordance with the Registration of Documents Ordinance. [59-1947/section-10]

Also, after the action is instituted, the court may, in its discretion, order the plaintiff to deposit the purchase amount set out in the notice given under section 5. [59-1947/section-11]

If the plaintiff defaults in depositing that amount within the period allowed by the court, or within further periods allowed by the court not exceeding three months in the aggregate, the plaintiff’s action shall be struck off the roll of pending cases. [59-1947/section-11]

Applied here, because the plaintiff has not yet proved registration of the action as a lis pendens, notice or summons should not be issued until that proof is furnished. If the court orders a deposit for the plaintiff’s bona fides, it may require deposit of the purchase amount stated in the section 5 notice, and failure to deposit it within the allowed time can result in the action being struck off the roll of pending cases.

Rule: “A mortgage of a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot shall, if it is effected on or after the appointed day, be null and void notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law.” The “appointed day” is “the eleventh day of December, 1957.”

Application: The facts say that, after the appointed day, the owner of a tea estate mortgages a physically divided portion of that estate as a separate lot. That is a mortgage of “a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot” effected “on or after the appointed day.” Therefore, the mortgage is null and void.

No. The statute says that “No share in the common elements of a registered, Condominium Property or of a registered Semi Condominium Property shall be disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of such property.” So the share in the common elements cannot be disposed of separately while the condominium parcel is retained.

If the condominium parcel itself is transferred, “any alienation of any condominium parcel shall be deemed also to convey the undivided share of the owner in the common elements appertaining to that condominium parcel” even if the deed does not specifically mention it. So the common-elements share passes with the parcel.

The rule is that “The Partition Law shall not apply to any land or building comprised in any registered Condominium Plan.” Applying that rule here, the property is land and a building already comprised in a registered Condominium Plan, so the Partition Law does not apply to it.

Under s 13, “No plan or map or copy or tracing of a plan or map shall be receivable in evidence in any court in Sri Lanka unless” it satisfies one of the stated preparation-and-certification routes.

The statutory text supplied provides these routes:
1. it has been “prepared … by or on behalf of the Surveyor-General by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him” and “certified by the Surveyor-General or by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him for such purpose”; or
2. it is “prepared … and certified by a registered licensed surveyor.”

So, a land plan tendered in civil proceedings is receivable only if it was prepared in one of those specified ways and certified in the corresponding specified way.

Yes. The provision says that any cadastral map, plan or other plan or map prepared in accordance with any written law, when it purports to be a true copy and purports to be signed by the Surveyor-General or an officer acting on his behalf, “shall be admissible evidence in all cases and for all purposes instead of the original.” It also says such a copy “may be taken as prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated there in as being that of the original.”

Applied here, the party’s copy purporting to be authenticated and signed by the Surveyor-General is admissible in place of the original. Its initial evidential status is prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated in it as being those of the original, until evidence to the contrary is given.

Rule: “it shall not be lawful for the company to register a transfer of shares ... unless a proper instrument of transfer has been delivered to the company.” So, on the facts of a voluntary transfer where no proper instrument of transfer has been delivered, the company may not register the transfer.

Exception: “nothing in this section shall affect any power of the company to register as shareholder ... any person to whom the right of any shares ... has been transmitted by operation of law.” So, if entitlement to the shares passes by operation of law, the company’s power to register that person as shareholder is preserved even though the section otherwise requires an instrument of transfer.

Under Companies Act, s 79, "A certificate signed under the name of the company by a director and secretary of the company specifying any shares held by any shareholder, shall be prima facie evidence of the title of the shareholder to the shares." Applied here, a share certificate in the company’s name signed by a director and the secretary, and specifying the shares held by the shareholder, is prima facie evidence that the recorded shareholder has title to those shares.

The statutory duties breached are:

1. The duty not to act, or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes the provisions contained in the company’s articles. Section 188 provides that “A director of a company shall not act or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes any provisions of this Act, or the provisions contained in the articles of the company.” On the facts, the director approved conduct that breaches the company’s articles, so this duty is breached.

2. The duty not to act in a manner which is reckless or grossly negligent. Section 189(a) says a director “shall not act in a manner which is reckless or grossly negligent.” On the facts, the director carried out the decision recklessly, so this duty is breached.

3. The duty to exercise the degree of skill and care that may reasonably be expected of a person of his knowledge and experience. Section 189(b) says a director “shall exercise the degree of skill and care that may reasonably be expected of a person of his knowledge and experience.” On the facts, the director acted without exercising that reasonable skill and care, so this duty is breached.

The rule is that “Any alienation of land effected in contravention of the provisions of this Act, shall be void and shall have no effect in law.” A “transfer” is included in the definition of “alienation,” which “means transfer, lease or mortgage of lands situated within Sri Lanka.”

Applied to the facts: because the transfer of land was completed in direct contravention of the Act, that alienation is void and has no effect in law.
